sources.title: American Civil War
sources.supportSnippet: The American Civil War (April 12, 1861 – May 26, 1865) was a civil war in the United States between the Union (states that remained loyal to the federal union) and the Confederacy (states that voted to secede). The central cause was the dispute over slavery. Key events include the attack on Fort Sumter, the Battle of Gettysburg, and the Confederate surrender at Appomattox Court House.

sources.title: Abraham Lincoln
sources.supportSnippet: Abraham Lincoln was the 16th president of the United States, serving from 1861 until his assassination in 1865. He led the Union through the American Civil War, defended the nation as a constitutional union, defeated the Confederacy, abolished slavery, and delivered the Gettysburg Address.

sources.title: The Emancipation Proclamation
sources.supportSnippet: Issued by President Abraham Lincoln on January 1, 1863, the Emancipation Proclamation declared 'that all persons held as slaves' within the rebellious states 'are, and henceforward shall be free.'

sources.title: U.S. Civics Test Questions and Answers (M-1778, 2025)
sources.supportSnippet: Q96 — What U.S. war ended slavery? Answer: the Civil War.

sources.title: 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution: Civil Rights (1868)
sources.supportSnippet: Passed by Congress June 13, 1866, and ratified July 9, 1868, the 14th Amendment extended liberties and rights granted by the Bill of Rights to former slaves and granted citizenship to all persons born or naturalized in the United States. The 13th Amendment (1865) had previously abolished slavery.

sources.title: Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution
sources.supportSnippet: Ratified February 3, 1870, the Fifteenth Amendment prohibits the federal government and each state from denying or abridging a citizen's right to vote on the basis of 'race, color, or previous condition of servitude.' For nearly a century after, many Black Americans were disenfranchised in the South, until the Voting Rights Act of 1965 enforced the amendment.

sources.title: Susan B. Anthony
sources.supportSnippet: Susan B. Anthony was an American social reformer and women's rights activist who played a pivotal role in the women's suffrage movement. With Elizabeth Cady Stanton she co-founded the National Woman Suffrage Association. Her work helped lead to the 19th Amendment in 1920, which gave women the right to vote.
